12510:
A polity is any group of people that is organized under a political structure — meaning the group has some system of governance, authority, and rules that control how it runs itself. It is the most general, all-purpose word in political vocabulary for a "governed community."

That's the heart of it. But the real beauty and usefulness of the word comes from understanding why it exists and what it does that no other word does quite as well.

Most words we use for governed communities are specific. "Country" calls to mind a modern nation with official borders and a flag. "Empire" implies conquest and vast territories. "Kingdom" implies a king. "City-state" is tied to a particular historical form. Each of these words locks you into a specific time, size, or structure.

"Polity" does not. It is the umbrella term that sits above all of these. It is deliberately broad and neutral, designed to refer to any organized political community regardless of its size, era, structure, or form. Scholars and political thinkers needed a word that could describe Athens in 400 BC and France in 2026 with equal accuracy, without the baggage that more specific words carry. That word is "polity."

Ancient Athens was a polity. The Roman Empire was a polity. A medieval kingdom in Europe was a polity. A modern democratic republic like Germany is a polity. A small tribal confederation in a remote region is a polity. What all of these share is a group of people organized under some system of political authority — and that shared quality is precisely what "polity" captures.

There is no minimum size requirement. A polity can be a tiny autonomous community of a few hundred people or a vast nation of hundreds of millions. What matters is not the scale but the presence of political organization.

"Polity" is used in two closely related but distinct ways, and you will encounter both.

The first sense refers to the community itself — the politically organized group of people, viewed as a single unit. Here, "polity" names the entity, the thing that exists in the world. Saying "Athens was a polity" uses it this way. You could substitute phrases like "political community" or "organized state" without losing much meaning.

The second sense refers to the form or system of government — how a community is structured politically. Here, asking "What polity does this society have?" means asking "What kind of political arrangement governs this society — a democracy, a monarchy, an oligarchy?" In this sense, "polity" is closer to "form of government."

In practice, both meanings often blend together, because a community and its system of governance are deeply intertwined. The context of the sentence will usually make it clear which sense is intended.

For something to count as a polity, it generally needs three things: a group of people (citizens, subjects, or members of some kind), some form of authority or governance (laws, rulers, institutions, or decision-making structures), and a degree of political organization — meaning it is not just a random crowd or a purely social group, but a structured community with rules and power arrangements.

It does not need to be a recognized nation-state. It does not need to be large or powerful. It simply needs to be politically organized in some meaningful way.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Understanding "polity" becomes much sharper when you compare it to the words it is often confused with.

A country or nation carries everyday, informal weight and typically implies a recognized modern state with fixed borders and an international identity. "Polity" is more scholarly and neutral, and it applies equally well to ancient or unconventional forms of political organization that we would not call a "country."

A state, in political science, often refers more narrowly to the governing institutions and apparatus of power — the machinery of rule. "Polity" tends to refer to the whole community, encompassing the people and their governance together. The state is something within a polity; the polity is the broader organized community.

A government is the ruling body that makes and enforces decisions within a polity. It is a part of a polity, not the same thing as a polity. The government governs; the polity is what is governed (along with the system that does the governing).

A society is a group of people sharing culture, norms, and social bonds, but it does not necessarily have political organization. A polity is specifically about political structure. All polities exist within societies, but not all societies are polities.
Who Uses This Word and When

"Polity" lives primarily in political science, political philosophy, history, and academic writing. It is not a word of everyday conversation. Scholars reach for it when they want to discuss a governed community in a way that is neutral and broad — not committed to any specific era, structure, or form.

For instance, a historian might write: "How did early human polities transition from small kinship-based groups to large territorial states?" This lets them discuss tribes, chiefdoms, city-states, and kingdoms all in one breath, under a single clean term, without having to specify or limit the type of political community being discussed.

A polity is any community of people — of any size, in any era — that is organized under a system of political authority and governance, from an ancient city-state to a modern nation-state to a small tribal community.
12511:
A polling place is an official, physical location where eligible voters go to cast their votes during an election. It is the specific building or site that has been set up, organized, and authorized by the government for the purpose of collecting votes from the public on a particular day.

Think of it this way: when a country, state, or local area holds an election — to choose a president, a mayor, a member of parliament, or to vote on a specific issue — people cannot just vote from anywhere they like. The government designates specific, controlled locations where voting must take place. These locations are called polling places.
What a Polling Place Looks Like

A polling place is not a special building built just for elections. Instead, authorities convert an existing public building into a polling place temporarily. Common examples include:

  • Schools (especially gymnasiums or halls)
  • Public libraries
  • Community centers
  • Churches or temples
  • Government offices
  • Fire stations
  • Sports halls

When you walk into a polling place on election day, you will typically see:

  • Check-in tables, where officials verify your identity and confirm you are registered to vote
  • Voting booths — small, enclosed cubicles or partitioned spaces that give you privacy while you mark your vote
  • Ballot boxes or voting machines, where you submit your completed vote
  • Poll workers — ordinary people trained to assist voters and ensure the process runs smoothly

The environment is deliberately calm, organized, and supervised.
How a Polling Place Works: Step by Step

When a voter goes to a polling place, here is what typically happens:

  1. You arrive at the designated location.
  2. You identify yourself — in many countries, you show an ID card or a voter registration card to confirm who you are.
  3. Your name is checked against the official list of registered voters for that area.
  4. You receive a ballot — a printed or electronic form listing the candidates or questions you must vote on.
  5. You go to a private voting booth to mark your choices, away from others.
  6. You submit your completed ballot — either by putting it into a sealed box, feeding it into a counting machine, or pressing a button on a touchscreen.
  7. You leave. In some places, you receive a small sticker or token as proof that you voted.

The entire process is designed to be secret (nobody should see how you voted), fair (everyone eligible gets exactly one vote), and orderly (it is supervised and recorded).
Who Can Use a Polling Place

Not everyone can walk into any polling place. In most electoral systems, each eligible voter is assigned to a specific polling place based on where they live. The geographic area a polling place serves is called a precinct, ward, or constituency (depending on the country). If you show up at the wrong polling place, you may be turned away or given a limited ballot.

To use a polling place at all, you typically need to be:

  • A citizen of the country (or eligible resident, in some local elections)
  • Of the minimum voting age (18 in most countries)
  • Registered to vote — meaning you have officially signed up with the government in advance

Polling places serve several critical purposes:

1. They ensure fairness and security.
Because voting happens at a supervised, official location, it is much harder for someone to cheat — for example, by voting multiple times, forcing others to vote a certain way, or tampering with results. Officials are present at all times.

2. They protect the secrecy of your vote.
The private booths inside a polling place ensure that nobody — not your employer, not your family member, not a political party — can see how you voted. This freedom is a cornerstone of democratic elections.

3. They make counting easier.
When votes are cast at specific, controlled locations, authorities can organize, collect, and count them in a structured way. Each polling place can report its results to the central election authority.

4. They make voting accessible.
Polling places are spread across a region so that voters do not have to travel a very long distance to cast their vote. Ideally, there should be a polling place within a reasonable distance of every neighborhood.

A polling place is only open on specific days set by law. The most important day is called Election Day — the official day when voting takes place. In many countries, Election Day is a public holiday so people can take time off to vote. Polling places usually open early in the morning (e.g., 7 AM) and close in the evening (e.g., 8 PM).

Some countries also allow early voting — a period of several days before the official Election Day when certain polling places are open so that people who cannot come on Election Day can vote in advance.

Once a polling place closes, no more votes are accepted. The votes cast there are then counted, either at the location itself or at a central counting facility.

It helps to clarify what a polling place is not:

  • It is not a permanent government office — it exists as a voting site only on election days.
  • It is not where you register to vote — registration is done in advance, usually at a government office, online, or by mail.
  • It is not the place where results are announced — results are calculated centrally, after all votes from all polling places in an area are collected and counted.
  • It is not the same as a mail-in or absentee ballot — some voters are allowed to vote by post and never visit a polling place at all, but that is a separate system.

TermWhat It Means
Polling stationEssentially the same as polling place; used more commonly in British English
Voting boothThe small private cubicle inside a polling place where you mark your ballot
BallotThe official form (paper or electronic) on which you record your vote
PrecinctThe geographic zone assigned to a particular polling place
Poll worker / Election officialA person trained to run the polling place on election day
Voter roll / Electoral registerThe official list of people eligible to vote, checked at the polling place
Early voting centerA polling place that opens before Election Day for advance voting

• "All registered voters in this neighborhood should report to the polling place at Lincoln Elementary School."
  • "Long queues formed outside the polling place as citizens waited to cast their votes in the presidential election."
  • "The polling place will open at 7 AM and close at 9 PM on Election Day."
  • "She had never missed an election and arrived at the polling place the moment it opened."
  • "Due to flooding, the local authorities moved the polling place from the community center to a nearby church."

A polling place is an officially designated, supervised, and temporary voting site — usually a public building — where eligible, registered voters go on election day to cast their votes privately and securely. It is the physical heart of a democratic election: the specific spot where a citizen's voice is formally recorded. Without polling places (or their alternatives like mail-in voting), there would be no organized, fair, or verifiable way to hold an election.
12512:
To pollute something means to make it dirty, harmful, or impure by introducing something that does not belong there — something that causes damage or makes it unsafe.

Think of it this way: imagine a glass of clean, clear water. Now imagine someone drops a spoonful of poison into it. The water is no longer safe. It has been polluted. That act — introducing something harmful into something that was previously clean or safe — is exactly what "pollute" means.

The most important thing to understand is that polluting always involves two things: something that was clean or acceptable, and something harmful that enters it and ruins it.
The Most Common Use — The Physical World

In everyday life, "pollute" is most often used to describe what humans do to nature:

  • Factories pollute rivers by dumping chemical waste into them.
  • Cars and industries pollute the air by releasing harmful gases.
  • Plastic garbage pollutes the ocean.
  • Oil spills pollute the sea and kill marine life.

In these cases, the thing being polluted (the river, the air, the ocean) was originally in a natural, usable state. The harmful substance introduced (chemicals, gases, plastic, oil) makes it dangerous, unclean, or unfit for life.

Notice that the word puts the blame on the one doing the act. If you say "the river was polluted," you are saying someone or something caused that harm. It is not a neutral word — it carries a strong sense that something wrong has happened.
You Can Pollute Many Different Things

While nature is the most common context, "pollute" is not limited to rivers and air. You can pollute anything that can be made impure or harmful:

  • Water — the most classic use. Chemicals, sewage, or waste entering drinking water or natural water bodies pollutes them.
  • Air — smoke, toxic gases, and particles pollute the air we breathe.
  • Soil/Land — pesticides, industrial chemicals, and waste can pollute the ground, making it infertile or toxic.
  • Food — contaminants or bacteria can pollute food, making it unsafe to eat.

The common thread in all these: something pure or usable is made harmful by the introduction of a foreign, damaging substance.
The Figurative Use — Beyond the Physical World

"Pollute" is also used in a non-physical, figurative sense. Here, it means to corrupt, spoil, or taint something non-physical — like a mind, a culture, a relationship, or an idea.

  • Hate speech can pollute public conversation by filling it with anger and division.
  • Greed pollutes a person's values — it takes something once decent and corrupts it.
  • Misinformation pollutes the mind by filling it with false beliefs.
  • A scandal can pollute a person's reputation.

In this figurative sense, the logic is exactly the same: something that was decent, clean, or functioning well is made worse — even "toxic" — by the introduction of something harmful. The word is used here metaphorically, borrowing from the physical idea of contamination and applying it to the moral or social world.

"Pollute" is not a mild word. It implies serious, damaging contamination — not just a small mess. If someone spills a bit of mud in a river, you would not normally say they "polluted" it. But if a factory releases thousands of litres of toxic chemicals into that same river, killing fish and making the water undrinkable — that is pollution.

This means "pollute" carries weight. Using it tells your listener or reader that the damage is significant and harmful, not trivial.

It is worth being clear about what this word does not mean, so you do not confuse it with similar-sounding ideas:

  • It does not simply mean "to make messy." Your bedroom being untidy is not pollution. The word requires that something harmful or toxic is introduced.
  • It does not mean "to destroy completely." Polluting something makes it impure or harmful, but the thing often still exists — it is just damaged or unsafe. A polluted river is still a river.
  • It is not the same as "to waste." Wasting something means using it carelessly. Polluting means contaminating it.
Important Related Words You Should Know

Understanding these connected words will complete your picture of "pollute":

  • Pollution (noun) — the result or state of being polluted. "Air pollution is a serious global problem." This is the condition that "polluting" causes.
  • Pollutant (noun) — the actual substance that does the polluting. Carbon dioxide, mercury, and plastic are all pollutants — they are the "harmful things introduced" that we talked about at the start.
  • Polluted (adjective) — describes something that has already been polluted. "The polluted river smelled terrible."
  • Polluter (noun) — a person, company, or thing that pollutes. "The factory was identified as the main polluter."
How to Use "Pollute" in a Sentence (Many Examples)

Here are varied examples so you can see how flexible the word is:

Physical:

  • "The chemical plant has been polluting the groundwater for decades."
  • "Diesel engines pollute the air more than electric vehicles."
  • "Sewage from the city was polluting the nearby beach."
  • "Runoff from farms pollutes streams with fertilizer chemicals."

Figurative:

  • "Violence in video games does not necessarily pollute a child's mind, according to many researchers."
  • "His bitter attitude began to pollute the mood of the entire team."
  • "Propaganda is designed to pollute the way people think about their enemies."
The Big Picture — One Sentence Summary

If you ever need to recall the meaning instantly: to pollute is to introduce something harmful into something previously clean or safe, making it toxic, impure, or damaged — whether that is a river, the air, a food supply, or even a person's mind or a society's values.
12513: A poltergeist is a type of ghost or supernatural spirit that is believed to cause physical disturbances in the real world — things like moving objects, making loud noises, breaking things, or switching lights on and off. The key idea is that a poltergeist is active and disruptive. It doesn't just appear and scare you by being visible — it physically interferes with your surroundings.
The core idea: an invisible troublemaker

Think of it this way. Most people imagine a ghost as a glowing, transparent figure that floats around and haunts a place. A poltergeist is different. You almost never see it. Instead, you experience it through what it does:

  • A book flies off a shelf on its own.
  • Doors slam shut with nobody near them.
  • You hear loud banging or knocking from inside the walls, with no source.
  • Furniture gets moved overnight.
  • Dishes shatter by themselves.

The poltergeist is the invisible force behind these events. It is mischievous, chaotic, and sometimes frightening — not because of how it looks, but because of how it acts.

The word is used in two main ways:

1. In the context of the supernatural and paranormal

This is its most common use. When people report strange, unexplained physical events in a house — objects moving on their own, weird sounds, things being thrown — they often describe the cause as a poltergeist. It's a term used in ghost stories, horror folklore, paranormal investigations, and supernatural beliefs.

"The family was terrified. Every night, the poltergeist would knock things off the kitchen counter and rattle the windows."

"Ghost hunters believe a poltergeist is responsible for the activity in the old mansion."

2. As a metaphor in everyday language

Sometimes people use "poltergeist" loosely and humorously to describe anything invisible that seems to cause chaos or mess — like blaming a poltergeist when you can't find something you just put down.

"I swear there's a poltergeist in this office — my keys keep disappearing."

This usage is informal and playful, not literal.
How a poltergeist is different from a regular ghost

This distinction is important and often confused.

ConceptRegular ghostPoltergeist

A regular ghost is typically associated with the spirit of a dead person. It might appear visually, revisit places it knew in life, or try to communicate. It's connected to a specific person's identity and history.

A poltergeist, on the other hand, is defined entirely by its behaviour, not its identity. Nobody knows "who" a poltergeist is or was. The focus is entirely on the chaos it creates. It is disruptive rather than communicative, physical rather than visual, and impersonal rather than tied to a specific person's story.

In short: a ghost appears, a poltergeist acts.
The tone and feeling of the word

"Poltergeist" carries a strong sense of unease, chaos, and the inexplicable. It suggests a force that is:

  • Invisible — you can't see it
  • Physical — but it affects the physical world
  • Unpredictable — you don't know when or where it will strike next
  • Mischievous to malicious — ranging from annoying to genuinely threatening

In storytelling and horror, a poltergeist often represents a force that is out of control and cannot be easily stopped or understood. It creates a particular kind of dread — not the fear of seeing something scary, but the fear of things happening on their own around you.

• "The old farmhouse was said to be haunted by a poltergeist that smashed plates and overturned furniture every full moon."
  • "She became convinced a poltergeist was in her apartment after her phone repeatedly flew off the table by itself."
  • "In paranormal research, a poltergeist is often investigated through recording unexplained sounds and tracking moved objects."
  • "The horror film featured a poltergeist so powerful it dragged furniture across the floor while the family watched in horror."

A poltergeist is an invisible, disruptive supernatural force — believed to throw objects, make loud noises, and cause physical chaos — distinguished from a typical ghost by its actions rather than its appearance.
12514: A poltroon is a person who is a complete and utter coward — not just a little nervous or hesitant, but someone who is shamefully and contemptibly cowardly. The word does not describe someone who simply feels fear. Fear is human, and everyone feels it. A poltroon is someone who lets fear completely control them and, as a result, behaves in a way that others find deeply disgraceful and worthy of scorn.

If you call someone a "coward," you are saying they lack courage. That is already a criticism. But if you call someone a poltroon, you are going several steps further. You are saying:

  • Their cowardice is extreme — not mild or forgivable.
  • Their cowardice is shameful — it reflects poorly on their character.
  • They deserve contempt — not sympathy, not understanding, but scorn.

The word carries a heavy moral judgment. It implies that the person had a duty or an opportunity to be brave — perhaps to stand up for someone, to face a challenge, or to do the right thing — and they miserably and despicably failed to do so, choosing self-preservation or avoidance over honour, courage, or responsibility.
The kind of behaviour it describes

A poltroon typically:

  • Runs away or backs down from danger, conflict, or difficulty when they are expected to stand firm.
  • Abandons others — friends, allies, people who needed them — to save their own skin.
  • Refuses to face consequences of their own actions, hiding or lying instead.
  • Shrinks from any confrontation, even when confrontation is clearly the right and necessary thing to do.

The key thing is that a poltroon's cowardice is active and visible to others — it is not a private, hidden feeling of fear, but a public display of spinelessness that leaves people around them disgusted.
The tone and register of the word

Poltroon is an old-fashioned, literary word. You will not typically hear it in everyday modern conversation — it belongs more to classic literature, historical fiction, poetry, formal writing, or dramatic speech. Think of a general on a battlefield calling a deserting soldier a poltroon, or a Victorian novelist describing a villain who abandons a woman in distress.

Because of its archaic quality, when the word is used in modern writing or speech, it often has one of two tones:

  1. Dramatic and serious — used to express strong, genuine contempt for someone's cowardice in a forceful, old-world way.
  2. Humorous or theatrical — used with a slightly tongue-in-cheek feel, because the word sounds so grand and old-fashioned that calling someone a poltroon today can come across as deliberately theatrical or even playfully mock-serious.

• "He called himself a leader, but when danger arrived, he fled without a second thought — a true poltroon."
  • "History has not been kind to him; he is remembered as a poltroon who abandoned his men in their darkest hour."
  • "Don't be such a poltroon — stand up and tell the truth."
  • "The crowd jeered at the poltroon who had promised to fight but surrendered at the very first sign of resistance."

A useful mental image: imagine a soldier who, the moment battle begins, throws down his weapon and runs. Or a person who witnesses an injustice and, despite being the only one who could speak up, stays silent and looks away. Or a man who makes a bold promise, then quietly disappears when it's time to deliver. That is a poltroon.

The word captures not just the act of being afraid, but the moral failure that comes from letting that fear make you useless, unreliable, and disgraceful to others who were counting on you.

A poltroon isA person of extreme, shameful, contemptible cowardice
It impliesMoral failure, disgrace, and worthy of scorn
It is stronger than "coward"because it carries active contempt, not just a neutral label
It is used inliterary, formal, historical, or dramatically expressive contexts

The single most important thing to remember: a poltroon is not just afraid — a poltroon fails others because of that fear, and does so in a way that earns them lasting shame and ridicule.
12515:
A polygamist is a person who is married to more than one spouse at the same time.

That last part — at the same time — is the heart of the word. It has nothing to do with marrying someone, getting divorced, and then marrying someone else. That is perfectly normal and legal in most of the world. A polygamist, by contrast, holds two or more active marriages simultaneously, meaning all those marriages exist together, at once, while they are all ongoing.
The Simplest Way to Picture It

Imagine a man named Arjun who is currently married to both Priya and Meena at the same time — not one after the other, but both at once, right now, today. Arjun is a polygamist.

Or imagine a woman named Sarah who is simultaneously the legal or recognized wife of both David and James. Sarah, too, is a polygamist.
The Two Main Forms a Polygamist Can Take

A polygamist's situation almost always fits into one of two specific patterns:

1. One husband, multiple wives.
This is called polygyny, and it is by far the most common form of polygamy throughout history and across cultures. When most people picture a polygamist, this is what they imagine. A man who has two, three, or more wives — all at the same time — is practicing polygyny, and he is a polygamist.

2. One wife, multiple husbands.
This is called polyandry, and it is rare but real. A woman who is simultaneously married to more than one man is also a polygamist. This has existed historically in certain communities in Tibet, parts of India, and a few other places.

Both types make the person a polygamist. The word covers either direction.
How Is a Polygamist Different from a Bigamist?

This is a subtle but important distinction.

A bigamist is specifically someone who illegally and usually secretly marries a second person while still being legally married to the first. The bigamist deceives someone — perhaps their first spouse doesn't know, or the new marriage partner doesn't know about the existing one. It is always a crime, and it always involves fraud or deception.

A polygamist is a broader term. It simply describes someone who has multiple spouses at once, without saying anything about whether it is legal or illegal, or whether anyone is being deceived. The word is neutral about legality. It just describes the marital situation.

So: every bigamist is technically a polygamist, but not every polygamist is a bigamist. A polygamist in a society or religion where multiple marriages are openly recognized and accepted — where everyone involved knows and consents — is still a polygamist but is not a bigamist.
How Is a Polygamist Different from Someone Who Is "Polyamorous"?

Another useful comparison. A polyamorous person has multiple romantic or intimate relationships at once, with everyone's knowledge and consent. However, they are not necessarily married to all those partners. The relationships exist, but legal or formal marriage is not required.

A polygamist, by definition, is specifically about marriage — formal, recognized marriage to multiple people. Marriage is the key element.

A person can be polyamorous without being a polygamist (multiple relationships, no multiple marriages). And a polygamist is specifically someone for whom multiple marriages exist simultaneously.

Understanding where polygamists exist in the real world makes the word more concrete.

In some Muslim-majority countries, Islamic law (in certain interpretations) permits a man to have up to four wives, provided he can treat them all fairly and equally. In countries like Saudi Arabia, Egypt, or Indonesia, polygamy — and therefore polygamists — exist legally. A man in such a society with three wives is openly, legally a polygamist.

In some fundamentalist Mormon communities in the United States and Canada, polygamy is practiced as a religious tradition, even though it is not recognized by the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (which banned it in 1890) and is illegal under civil law. Men in these communities who have multiple wives consider themselves religiously married, making them polygamists in practice.

In various African and indigenous cultures, multiple wives have historically been a mark of wealth or status, and polygamy remains practiced in many communities.

In most Western countries — the UK, US, France, India (for non-Muslims under civil law), etc. — polygamy is illegal. A polygamist in these places cannot legally register more than one marriage. If someone tries to, they become a bigamist in the eyes of the law.
Can a Woman Be a Polygamist?

Absolutely, yes. The word polygamist applies to any person — man or woman — who is simultaneously married to more than one spouse. It is not a gendered word. A woman with two husbands is every bit as much a polygamist as a man with two wives.

In practice, across most human history and most cultures where polygamy has existed, it has been men with multiple wives, not women with multiple husbands. But the word itself does not restrict by gender.

To make sure the word feels natural, here are a few example sentences:

  • "He was a known polygamist who had four wives living in the same village."
  • "The law in that country forbids any citizen from becoming a polygamist."
  • "She did not know her husband was already married — she had unknowingly become part of a polygamist's household."
  • "Some polygamists argue that all their marriages are consensual and should be a private matter."

If you had to capture the entire meaning in one sentence:

A polygamist is a person who is married to more than one spouse at the same time.

Everything else — the types, the legal nuances, the cultural contexts — flows out from that single core idea.
12516:
Polygamy is a noun. It refers to the practice of being married to more than one spouse — a husband or a wife — at the exact same time. It is the opposite of monogamy, which means being married to only one person at a time.

Think of it this way: in a monogamous marriage, there are exactly two people — one husband and one wife (or one partner and another). In a polygamous marriage, one person is legally or culturally married to two or more people simultaneously.

Polygamy is actually an umbrella term. It has three distinct forms underneath it, and knowing them prevents a lot of confusion.

Polygyny is by far the most common form. This is when one man has multiple wives at the same time. For example, a man married to three women simultaneously is practicing polygyny. When most people say "polygamy" in everyday conversation, they usually mean this.

Polyandry is the opposite and is quite rare in human history. This is when one woman has multiple husbands at the same time. It has been practiced in a few societies historically, such as in certain communities in Tibet and parts of South Asia.

Group marriage (sometimes called polygynandry) is when multiple men and multiple women are all married to each other within one shared union. This is the rarest form and exists in very few cultural contexts.
What Makes It "Polygamy" and Not Something Else

A crucial detail: polygamy specifically involves marriage — a formal, recognized bond, whether by law, religion, or strong cultural custom. It is not simply about having romantic or sexual relationships with multiple people outside of marriage. The "marriage" aspect is what defines it.

This is also what separates polygamy from polyamory. Polyamory refers to having multiple romantic relationships with the knowledge and consent of everyone involved, but it does not necessarily involve marriage. Polygamy, by contrast, is specifically about the marital structure.

Another related word you may encounter is bigamy. Bigamy is when someone gets married to a second person while already being legally married to the first — without dissolving the first marriage, and often without the first spouse knowing. Bigamy is considered deceptive and is a crime in most countries. Polygamy, in the contexts where it is practiced, is typically an open, accepted arrangement known to everyone involved.
Where and Why It Is Practiced

Polygamy has existed across many cultures and religions throughout human history. Today, it is most commonly associated with certain interpretations of Islam, which permits a man to have up to four wives under specific conditions (including the requirement to treat all wives equally and fairly). It is also practiced in some communities of Fundamentalist Mormon sects in the United States, though mainstream Mormonism banned it in 1890. Additionally, polygamy exists in parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia as a cultural or tribal tradition.

It is worth understanding that in societies where polygamy is practiced, it is usually tied to economic, social, or religious frameworks — not simply personal desire. In some agricultural communities historically, for instance, having multiple wives was linked to labor, land ownership, and family alliances.

Polygamy is illegal in most Western countries, including the United States, Canada, Australia, and across Europe. Practicing it there can result in criminal charges.

However, polygamy is legal and socially accepted in several countries, particularly across parts of Africa and the Middle East. Countries like Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, and Nigeria (in states operating under Islamic law) permit it, usually with certain restrictions.
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

Here are a few natural examples to show you how "polygamy" functions as a noun in real language:

  • "Polygamy is legal in some countries but illegal in others."
  • "The documentary explored the lives of women living in polygamy."
  • "He studied the role of polygamy in ancient societies."
  • "She strongly opposed polygamy on the grounds of gender equality."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: polygamy = being married to more than one spouse at the same time. Everything else — the types, the contexts, the legality — branches out from that single core idea.
12517:
When polyglot is used as an adjective, it means "involving, using, or expressed in several languages." It describes anything — a person, a place, a book, a community — that operates across multiple languages at once.

The key word is several. Not one, not even just two, but many.

A polyglot person is someone who knows and uses several languages, often with a reasonable degree of skill in each.

"She is a polyglot scholar who conducts research in French, Arabic, and Mandarin."

Here, polyglot tells you she doesn't just dabble in those languages — she actively works across all of them.
When It Describes a Place or Community

A city, region, or community can be described as polyglot when many different languages are spoken there, often side by side in daily life.

"Singapore is a famously polyglot society, where English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil are all official languages."

"The border town had a polyglot population — you could hear five different languages at the market on any given morning."

In this sense, it paints a picture of linguistic richness and diversity in a place.
When It Describes a Text or Document

A book, manuscript, or document is called polyglot when its content is written in several languages, often presenting the same material in each language in parallel columns or sections.

"The researchers consulted a polyglot edition of the ancient text, which displayed the original Greek alongside Latin and Hebrew translations."

This is a very specific and common use in academic and religious contexts — for example, polyglot Bibles were historically produced to display scripture in multiple languages at once, for the purpose of scholarly comparison.

These three words exist on a spectrum, and it helps to know where polyglot sits:

  • Bilingual — two languages only.
  • Multilingual — more than two languages (a general, broad term).
  • Polyglot — also more than two languages, but the word tends to suggest an impressive number and often implies active, skilled use of those languages — not just exposure or basic familiarity. It carries a slightly more elevated or emphatic tone than "multilingual."

You could call a country with three official languages "multilingual" — but you'd call a diplomat who negotiates fluently in seven languages "polyglot." It has a sense of breadth and depth.

Polyglot is not a neutral, clinical word. It tends to carry a sense of richness, sophistication, and variety. When a writer describes a city or a person as polyglot, there is often an undertone of admiration or wonder — a recognition that something impressive and layered is happening across multiple linguistic worlds at once.

ContextExample Sentence
Person"The polyglot ambassador addressed each delegation in their native tongue."
City"Montreal has a polyglot character, shaped by waves of immigration."
Text"He studied a polyglot manuscript containing passages in five ancient languages."
Environment"The conference was a polyglot affair, with simultaneous interpretation running in eight languages."
How to Spot It in the Wild

When you see polyglot used as an adjective, ask yourself: "What is it describing?" Then ask: "Does that thing involve multiple languages?" If yes, the word is being used correctly. It could be describing the linguistic makeup of a person's mind, a city's culture, a document's structure, or an environment's atmosphere — but in every case, the thread is the same: many languages, coexisting.
12518: A polyglot is a person who knows and can use multiple languages — typically defined as three or more. The key word here is use. A polyglot doesn't just recognize a few phrases from a foreign movie or remember some words from a class years ago. They can actually operate in those languages — reading, writing, speaking, or understanding them at a meaningful level.
What "Knowing" a Language Really Means Here

This is important: not every polyglot knows all their languages equally well. A polyglot might:

  • Be fluent in some languages (speaking naturally, like a native or near-native speaker)
  • Be proficient in others (handling most conversations and reading with ease)
  • Have working knowledge in others still (able to get things done, hold conversations, read basic texts)

All of this still counts. A polyglot is not required to be perfect in every language they know. What matters is that they have a genuine, functional command of multiple languages — not just a tourist's handful of phrases.
How Many Languages Does It Take?

There is no strict, universally agreed-upon number, but the word is almost always used for three or more languages. Here's a rough way to think about it:

  • Someone who knows one language is called a monolingual.
  • Someone who knows two languages is called a bilingual.
  • Someone who knows two or more is sometimes called multilingual (a broader term).
  • Someone who knows three or more with genuine ability is typically called a polyglot.

Some people reserve the word for those with a particularly impressive number — say, five, six, or more — but in everyday and formal use, three or more is the widely accepted starting point.

There is also an extreme version: a person who knows a dozen or more languages at a high level is sometimes called a hyperpolyglot, though this term is less common and more informal.

The word carries a sense of active ability and real-world use, not just academic study. For example:

  • A professor who spent 40 years studying Ancient Greek grammar but cannot hold a conversation might not be called a polyglot in the truest sense.
  • A person who grew up in a multilingual household, traveled extensively, and can fluidly switch between English, French, Mandarin, and Arabic? That person is a textbook polyglot.

The emphasis is on communicative ability — the languages live in the person, not just on paper.

Here are some examples that show how the word naturally appears:

  • "She grew up in Brussels, then lived in Tokyo and São Paulo — she's quite the polyglot."
  • "The diplomat was a renowned polyglot, conducting meetings in four different languages without an interpreter."
  • "You don't have to be a polyglot to travel, but it certainly helps."
  • "He's a polyglot who speaks English, Spanish, German, and Swahili fluently."

To make the concept vivid and concrete, here are some historically famous polyglots:

  • Cleopatra (the Egyptian queen) reportedly spoke nine languages, which was historically remarkable and politically powerful.
  • Giuseppe Caspar Mezzofanti, a 19th-century Italian cardinal, was said to speak 38 languages fluently — one of the most celebrated polyglots in recorded history.
  • Pope John Paul II conducted audiences in Polish, Italian, French, German, English, Spanish, Portuguese, and several other languages.
  • J.R.R. Tolkien, the author of The Lord of the Rings, was a trained linguist who knew over a dozen languages, including ancient and medieval ones — and even invented his own.
A Common Misconception to Watch Out For

Being a polyglot is not the same as being a translator or interpreter (though some polyglots are those things professionally). A polyglot is simply a person who knows many languages. What they do with those languages professionally or personally is a separate matter entirely.

Think of a polyglot as someone whose mind holds multiple entire worlds of communication inside it. Each language is not just a set of words — it's a system of grammar, culture, idioms, rhythm, and nuance. A polyglot has meaningfully internalized three or more of these systems and can navigate between them. It is genuinely one of the most remarkable cognitive abilities a person can develop.

A polygon is a flat, closed shape made entirely of straight lines. That's the core of it. Every polygon lives on a flat surface (like a piece of paper), is completely closed with no openings or gaps, and has sides that are perfectly straight — no curves allowed.

The word is used for a very wide family of shapes. A triangle is a polygon. So is a square, a hexagon, and a stop sign shape. What they all share: flatness, closure, and straight sides.
The three rules a shape must follow to be a polygon

1. It must be flat (two-dimensional).
A polygon has no depth. It exists on a plane — like a shape drawn on paper. A cube or a sphere is not a polygon because they have three dimensions.

2. It must be closed.
All the sides must connect end-to-end with no gaps. If you trace the outline of a polygon, you'll always return to exactly where you started. An open shape — say, the letter "C" — is not a polygon.

3. All sides must be straight.
Not a single curved line is allowed. A circle is not a polygon. Neither is a shape with even one curved edge.
The parts of a polygon

Sides (also called edges): The straight line segments that form the boundary of the shape. Every polygon has at least three sides.

Vertices (singular: vertex): The corner points where two sides meet. A polygon has exactly as many vertices as it has sides. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 vertices. A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 vertices.

Interior angles: The angles formed inside the polygon at each vertex — where two sides meet on the inside. These angles tell you how "sharp" or "wide" each corner is.

Exterior angles: If you extend any side of a polygon beyond a vertex, the angle formed outside the shape between that extension and the next side is called an exterior angle.

Diagonals: A diagonal is a straight line drawn inside the polygon connecting two vertices that are not directly next to each other. A triangle has no diagonals (every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex). A quadrilateral has 2 diagonals. A pentagon has 5.
How polygons are named — by the number of sides

The number of sides is the most basic way to identify a polygon:

  • 3 sides → Triangle
  • 4 sides → Quadrilateral (this includes squares, rectangles, parallelograms, rhombuses, and trapezoids)
  • 5 sides → Pentagon
  • 6 sides → Hexagon
  • 7 sides → Heptagon
  • 8 sides → Octagon
  • 9 sides → Nonagon
  • 10 sides → Decagon
  • 12 sides → Dodecagon

For polygons with many sides that don't have a common name, mathematicians simply say n-gon, where n is the number of sides. So a 17-sided polygon is a 17-gon.
Regular vs. Irregular polygons

A regular polygon is one where all sides are equal in length AND all interior angles are equal in measure. Think of a perfect square (all four sides identical, all four angles exactly 90°), or an equilateral triangle (all three sides equal, all three angles exactly 60°), or a regular hexagon (the kind you see in a honeycomb). These shapes have a perfect, symmetric beauty to them.

An irregular polygon is everything else — where the sides are not all the same length, or the angles are not all equal, or both. A typical hand-drawn rectangle is actually a regular shape in terms of angles (all 90°) but irregular in terms of sides if it's longer than it is wide. Most real-world polygons are irregular.
Convex vs. Concave polygons

This is another important way to classify polygons.

A convex polygon is one where all the interior angles are less than 180°. If you stand inside a convex polygon and look outward, you always see the outside. No part of the shape "caves in" or "dips inward." A square, a regular pentagon, and a triangle are all convex. A useful test: if you pick any two points inside the shape and draw a line between them, that line stays entirely inside the shape.

A concave polygon has at least one interior angle that is greater than 180° (called a reflex angle). This causes the shape to appear to have an indentation or a "dent" — some part of it caves inward like an arrowhead or a star. If you pick two points inside a concave polygon, the line between them might pass outside the shape.
Simple vs. Self-intersecting polygons

A simple polygon has sides that never cross over each other. The boundary traces a clean, non-overlapping path. Almost every polygon you'll encounter in everyday life is simple.

A self-intersecting polygon (also called a complex polygon) has sides that cross each other. The classic example is a five-pointed star (pentagram): if you draw it as one continuous path, the sides cross. These are less common but technically still qualify as polygons in formal mathematics.
The sum of interior angles

Here's something elegant: the sum of all interior angles in any polygon follows a reliable formula.

For a polygon with n sides:

Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°

  • Triangle (3 sides): (3 − 2) × 180° = 180°
  • Quadrilateral (4 sides): (4 − 2) × 180° = 360°
  • Pentagon (5 sides): (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°
  • Hexagon (6 sides): (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°

This formula works for any simple polygon, no matter how irregular it looks. You can verify it yourself by drawing any quadrilateral, cutting out its four corners, and arranging them together — they'll always form a perfect 360° circle.

For a regular polygon, since all angles are equal, each individual interior angle = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n.
Perimeter and area

The perimeter of a polygon is simply the total length of all its sides added together. If a triangle has sides of length 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm, its perimeter is 12 cm.

The area is the amount of flat space enclosed inside the polygon. Calculating area depends on the type of polygon. Triangles, rectangles, and regular polygons all have their own formulas. For irregular polygons, one common technique is to divide the shape into simpler polygons (like triangles), calculate each area, and add them up.
What is NOT a polygon

• A circle — it has no straight sides at all
  • An ellipse or oval — curved
  • Any open shape — a line segment, an arc, or a shape with a gap in it
  • Any three-dimensional shape — a cube, a cylinder, a pyramid (though the flat faces of a 3D shape can themselves be polygons)
  • Any shape with even one curved side
Polygons in real life

Polygons are everywhere once you start looking:

  • Triangle: a musical triangle instrument, a yield sign, a slice of pizza
  • Quadrilateral: book pages, doors, screens, windows, floor tiles
  • Pentagon: the famous Pentagon building in the USA (viewed from above)
  • Hexagon: cells in a honeycomb, some nuts and bolts (seen from the end)
  • Octagon: a stop sign
  • Irregular polygons: the shapes of countries on a map, floor plans of rooms, the outline of a leaf (if approximated with straight edges)
The big picture

A polygon is geometry's way of describing any enclosed, flat region whose boundary is made of straight-line segments. It is the foundation of shape in two dimensions. From the simple triangle to the thousand-sided polygon that looks almost like a circle, the concept stretches far while staying grounded in three non-negotiable rules: flat, closed, straight.
